# Sharing Functions with Code Libraries {#chapter-8-sharing-functions-with-code-libraries}

By now you should realize that the computer has to do a lot of work even
for simple tasks. Because of that, you have to do a lot of work to write
the code for a computer to even do simple tasks. In addition,
programming tasks are usually not very simple. Therefore, we need a way
to make this process easier on ourselves. There are several ways to do
this, including:

-   Write code in a high-level language instead of assembly language.

-   Have lots of pre-written code that you can cut and paste into your
    own programs.

-   Have a set of functions on the system that are shared among
    any program that wishes to use it.

All three of these are usually used to some degree in any given project.
The first option will be explored further in
[Chapter 11. High-Level Languages](11-high-level-languages.qmd#chapter-11-high-level-languages).
The second option is useful but it suffers from some drawbacks,
including:

-   Code that is copied often has to be majorly modified to fit the
    surrounding code.

-   Every program containing the copied code has the same code in it,
    thus wasting a lot of space.

-   If a bug is found in any of the copied code it has to be fixed in
    every application program.

Therefore, the second option is usually used sparingly. It is usually
only used in cases where you copy and paste skeleton code
for a specific type of task, and add in your program-specific details.
The third option is the one that is used the most often. The third
option includes having a central repository of shared code. Then,
instead of each program wasting space storing the same copies of
functions, they can simply point to the *shared libraries*
which contain the functions they need. If a
bug is found in one of these functions, it only has to be fixed within
the single function library file, and all applications which use it are
automatically updated. The main drawback with this approach is that it
creates some dependency problems, including:

-   If multiple applications are all using the same file, how do we know
    when it is safe to delete the file? For example, if three
    applications are sharing a file of functions and 2 of the programs
    are deleted, how does the system know that there still exists an
    application that uses that code, and therefore it shouldn\'t be
    deleted?

-   Some programs inadvertently rely on bugs within shared functions.
    Therefore, if upgrading the shared functions fixes a bug that a
    program depended on, it could cause that application to cease
    functioning.

These problems are what lead to what is known as \"DLL hell\". Linux
distributions solve most of them with package managers, which know
which programs need which libraries, and with version numbers in the
names of the libraries, as we will see. It is generally assumed that the
advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

In programming, these shared code files are referred to as *shared
libraries*, *dynamic libraries*, *shared objects*, *dynamic-link
libraries*, *DLLs*, or *.so files*.[^8-1] We will refer to all of
these as *shared libraries*.

This chapter uses the C library, the shared library that almost every
Linux program uses, and then builds shared libraries of our own. At the
end, we call our assembly functions from Rust and from Python. That is
the real reason to follow the calling convention of
[Chapter 4. All About Functions](04-all-about-functions.qmd#chapter-4-all-about-functions)
so carefully: any language that knows the convention can use our code.

Using a Shared Library {#using-a-shared-library}
----------------------

The program we will examine here is simple - it writes the characters
`hello world` to the screen and exits. The regular program,
`008-01-hello-world-nolib.s`, looks like this:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-01-hello-world-nolib.s}
```

That\'s not too long. However, take a look at how short
`008-01-hello-world-lib` is, which uses a library:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-01-hello-world-lib.s}
```

It\'s even shorter! It calls two functions of the C library: `printf`,
which prints text, and `exit`, which ends the program. They follow the
convention of Chapter 4, so the first parameter goes in _%rdi_. For
`printf` it is the address of the text, which ends with a null byte
(`\0`) instead of having its length in a separate register. Ignore the
`movq $0, %rax` and the `@PLT` after the names for now; we will explain
both soon.

Now, building programs which use shared libraries is a little
different than normal. You can build the first program normally by
doing this:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 008-01-hello-world-nolib.o 008-01-hello-world-nolib.s
ld -o 008-01-hello-world-nolib 008-01-hello-world-nolib.o
```

However, in order to build the second program, you have to do this:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 008-01-hello-world-lib.o 008-01-hello-world-lib.s
ld -o 008-01-hello-world-lib 008-01-hello-world-lib.o \
  -l c -dynamic-linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
```

Run both programs and you will get the classic message:

```{.bash}
./008-01-hello-world-lib
./008-01-hello-world-nolib
```

Remember, the backslash at the end of a line simply means that the
command continues on the next line. The option `-dynamic-linker
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` allows our program to be linked to
libraries. This builds the executable so that before executing, the
operating system will load the program `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` to
load in external libraries and link them with the program. This program
is known as a *dynamic linker*. Its path is the same on almost every
x86-64 Linux distribution.

The `-l c` (or `--library c`) option says to link to the C library,
named `libc.so` on GNU/Linux systems. Given a library name, `c` in this
case (usually library names are longer than a single letter), the
GNU/Linux linker prepends the string `lib` to the beginning of the
library name and appends `.so` to the end of it to form the library\'s
filename. This library contains many functions to automate all types of
tasks. The two we are using are `printf`, which prints strings, and
`exit`, which exits the program.

Why `exit` and not the `exit` system call we have always used? The C
library keeps the text of `printf` in a buffer, in memory, and writes
it to the file descriptor later, with a single `write`, which is much
faster than one system call per `printf`. The `exit` function writes
whatever is left in the buffers and then makes the system call. If we
ended the program with the system call directly, the text could be
lost.

Notice that the symbols `printf` and `exit` are simply referred to by
name within the program. In previous chapters, the linker would resolve
all of the names to memory addresses, and the names would be thrown
away. When using dynamic linking, the name itself resides within the
executable, and is resolved by the dynamic linker when it is run. When
the program is run by the user, the dynamic linker loads the shared
libraries listed in our link statement, and then finds all of the
function and variable names that were named by our program but not
found at link time, and matches them up with corresponding entries in
the shared libraries it loads. It then replaces all of the names with
the addresses which they are loaded at. This sounds time-consuming. It
is to a small degree, but it only happens once for each name.

How Shared Libraries Work {#how-shared-libraries-work}
-------------------------

In our first programs, all of the code was contained within the source
file. Such programs are called *statically-linked executables*, because
they contained all of the necessary functionality for the program that
wasn\'t handled by the kernel. In the programs we wrote in
[Chapter 6. Reading and Writing Simple Records](06-reading-and-writing-simple-records.qmd#chapter-6-reading-and-writing-simple-records),
we used both our main program file and files containing routines used
by multiple programs. In these cases, we combined all of the code
together using the linker at link-time, so it was still
statically-linked. However, in the `008-01-hello-world-lib` program, we
started using shared libraries. When you use shared libraries, your
program is then *dynamically-linked*, which means that not all of the
code needed to run the program is actually contained within the program
file itself, but in external libraries.

When we put the `-l c` on the command to link the
`008-01-hello-world-lib` program, it told the linker to use the C
library to look up any symbols that weren\'t already defined in
`008-01-hello-world-lib.o`. However, it doesn\'t actually add any code
to our program, it just notes in the program where to look. You can see
those notes with `readelf -d`, which prints the *dynamic section* of
the file. Its first line says:

     0x0000000000000001 (NEEDED)             Shared library: [libc.so.6]

The file that `ld` found was `libc.so`, but the note says `libc.so.6`.
On Ubuntu 24.04, `libc.so` is not a library but a small text file, a
script for the linker, which names the real library:

    GROUP ( /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc_nonshared.a  AS_NEEDED ( /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ) )

The `.6` is the version of the library\'s interface. If the C library
ever changed in a way that broke old programs, it would be called
`libc.so.7`, and the old programs would keep using `libc.so.6`. This is
one of the ways Linux avoids \"DLL hell\".

When the `008-01-hello-world-lib` program begins, the file
`/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` is loaded first. This is the dynamic
linker. This looks at our `008-01-hello-world-lib` program and sees that
it needs `libc.so.6` to run. So, it searches for that file: first in
the directories of the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable, if it is
set, then in the directories listed in `/etc/ld.so.conf`, and finally in
the system directories, such as `/lib` and `/usr/lib`. Then it looks in
it for all the needed symbols (`printf` and `exit` in this case), and
then loads the library into the program\'s virtual memory. Finally, it
connects every use of `printf` in the program with the actual location
of `printf` in the library.

The dynamic linker also prepares the C library itself before our
program starts. That is why our `_start` can call `printf` right away.
Programs written in C don\'t have a `_start` of their own: the compiler
adds one, which calls a function named `main`.

Run the following command:

```{.bash}
ldd ./008-01-hello-world-nolib
```

It should report back `not a dynamic executable`. This is just like we
said - `008-01-hello-world-nolib` is a statically-linked executable.
However, try this:

```{.bash}
ldd ./008-01-hello-world-lib
```

On Ubuntu 24.04 it reports:

    linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007fe52a56a000)
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007fe52a200000)
    /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007fe52a56c000)

The numbers in parentheses are the addresses where each library was
loaded, and they change every time you run it, because Linux loads
libraries at random addresses (we will see why in
[Chapter 9. Intermediate Memory Topics](09-intermediate-memory-topics.qmd#chapter-9.-intermediate-memory-topics)).
This means that the program `008-01-hello-world-lib` is linked to
`libc.so.6`, which is found at `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/` on Ubuntu (other
distributions use `/usr/lib/` or `/lib64/`), and that it needs the
dynamic linker. `linux-vdso.so.1` is not a file at all: it is a small
library that the kernel puts into every program, with a few functions
(such as reading the clock) that run without a real system call. If
you are interested, run the `ldd` program on various programs that are
on your Linux distribution, and see what libraries they rely on.

Two Rules for Calling Library Functions {#two-rules-for-calling-library-functions}
---------------------------------------

Our own functions only depend on each other, so a small mistake in the
calling convention may go unnoticed. The functions of a library were
compiled to follow the convention exactly, and they rely on two rules
that our functions never needed.

The first rule is the one from the note on stack alignment in
[Chapter 4](04-all-about-functions.qmd#chapter-4-all-about-functions):
_%rsp_ must be a multiple of 16 whenever a `call` instruction runs.
When Linux starts a program, _%rsp_ is already a multiple of 16, and
`008-01-hello-world-lib` doesn\'t push anything, so it is still aligned
at each `call`. A function with the usual `pushq %rbp` and locals in
blocks of 16 bytes is aligned too.

The second rule is for functions like `printf` that accept a variable
number of parameters. Some parameters, the floating-point numbers that
we will meet in
[Chapter 10. Counting Like a Computer](10-counting-like-a-computer.qmd#chapter-10-counting-like-a-computer),
go in other registers, the *vector registers* _%xmm0_ to _%xmm7_.
`printf` can\'t know in advance which of them hold parameters, so the
caller says how many it used in _%al_, the lowest byte of _%rax_. We
pass no floating-point numbers, so we put 0 there: `movq $0, %rax`.

What happens if you break them? We tried it with `008-02-printf-example`
(the next program), adding a `pushq $0` just before the call to
`printf` to break the alignment. On Ubuntu 24.04 (C library 2.39) the
program still worked when _%al_ was 0. With _%al_ set to 1, it crashed
with a segmentation fault. gdb shows the instruction that failed:

    => 0x7ff826260136 <printf+54>:  movaps %xmm0,-0x80(%rbp)

When _%al_ is not 0, `printf` starts by saving the vector registers on
its stack with `movaps`, an instruction that moves 16 bytes and requires
an address that is a multiple of 16. Notice that the program didn\'t
fail because of either rule alone: with the wrong alignment and _%al_
= 0 it worked by luck, and another version of the library could crash
in the same case. This is why both rules must be followed every time,
even when breaking them seems to work.

Finding Information about Libraries {#finding-information-about-libraries}
-----------------------------------

Okay, so now that you know about libraries, the question is, how do you
find out what libraries you have on your system and what they do? Well,
let\'s skip that question for a minute and ask another question: How do
programmers describe functions to each other in their documentation?
Let\'s take a look at the function `printf`. Its calling interface
(usually referred to as a *prototype*) looks like this:

```{.c}
int printf(const char *format, ...);
```

In Linux, functions are described in the C programming language. The
system and most of its libraries were written in C, so their
documentation, their header files and the calling convention itself
are defined in terms of C, which is why the convention is often called
the \"C ABI\". You don\'t need to know how to program in C to read a
prototype; you only need to know the meaning of a few words, which we
will see now. The same function in Rust would be declared like this:

```{.rust}
fn printf(format: *const c_char, ...) -> c_int;
```

This definition means that there is a function `printf`. The things
inside the parenthesis are the function\'s parameters or arguments. The
first parameter here is `const char *format`. This means there is a
parameter named `format` (the name isn\'t important, except to use for
talking about it), which has a type `char *`. `char` means that it
wants a single-byte character. The `*` after it means that it doesn\'t
actually want a character as an argument, but instead it wants the
address of a character or sequence of characters, and `const` means
that `printf` promises not to change them. If you look back at our
`008-01-hello-world-lib` program, you will notice that the function
call looked like this:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines snippet=008-01-hello-world-lib-leaq-helloworld-rip}
```

So, we passed the address of the `helloworld` string in _%rdi_, rather
than the actual characters. You might notice that we didn\'t pass the
length of the string. The way that `printf` found the end of the string
was because we ended it with a null character (`\0`). Many functions
work that way, especially C language functions. The `int` before the
function name tells what type of value the function will return in
_%rax_ when it returns. `printf` will return an `int` (the number of
bytes it printed) when it\'s through. Now, after the `const char
*format`, we have a series of periods, `...`. This means that it can
take an indefinite number of additional arguments after the string.
Most functions can only take a specified number of arguments. `printf`,
however, can take many. It will look into the `format` parameter, and
everywhere it sees the characters `%s`, it will look for another string
to insert, and everywhere it sees `%ld` it will look for a number to
insert. This is best described using an example,
`008-02-printf-example.s`:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-02-printf-example.s}
```

Type it in with the filename `008-02-printf-example.s`, and then do the
following commands:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 008-02-printf-example.o 008-02-printf-example.s
ld -o 008-02-printf-example 008-02-printf-example.o \
  -l c -dynamic-linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
```

Then run the program with `./008-02-printf-example`, and it should say
this:

    Hi! Jonathan is the person number #3.

The parameters go in _%rdi_, _%rsi_, _%rdx_ and _%rcx_, in the same
order as in the prototype: the format string first. If there were more
than six, the rest would go on the stack, as we saw in Chapter 4.[^8-2]
You may be wondering how the `printf` function knows how many
parameters there are. Well, it searches through your string, and counts
how many `%ld`s and `%s`s it finds, and then takes that number of
parameters from the registers (and the stack, if needed). If the
parameter matches a `%ld`, it treats it as a number, and if it matches
a `%s`, it treats it as a pointer to a null-terminated string. `printf`
has many more features than this, but these are the most-used ones. So,
as you can see, `printf` can make output a lot easier, but it also has
a lot of overhead, because it has to count the number of characters in
the string, look through it for all of the control characters it needs
to replace, take the parameters, convert them to a suitable
representation (numbers have to be converted to strings, etc), and
stick them all together appropriately.

Why `%ld` and not `%d`? `%d` is for an `int`, which is 4 bytes, and
`%ld` for a `long`, which is 8 bytes like our `.quad`. With `%d`,
`printf` would only look at _%ecx_, the lower half of _%rcx_. Our number
is small, so it would print the same thing, but a number bigger than
2,147,483,647 would come out wrong. The sizes matter, so let\'s see
them.

We\'ve seen how to use the C programming language prototypes to call
library functions. To use them effectively, however, you need to know
several more of the possible data types for reading functions. Here are
the main ones, with their sizes on 64-bit Linux and the equivalent
types in Rust and in the `ctypes` module of Python, which we will use
later in this chapter:

`char`:

:   A `char` is a single-byte integer number, from _-128_ to _127_
    (Rust `i8` or `c_char`; Python `ctypes.c_char`). This is mostly used
    for storing character data, since ASCII strings usually are
    represented with one byte per character.

`short`:

:   A `short` is an integer number of 2 bytes, from _-32,768_ to
    _32,767_ (Rust `i16`; Python `ctypes.c_short`).

`int`:

:   An `int` is an integer number of 4 bytes, from _-2,147,483,648_ to
    _2,147,483,647_ (Rust `i32`; Python `ctypes.c_int`). A function
    that returns an `int` only sets _%eax_, and a function that
    receives one only reads the lower 4 bytes of its register (for
    example, _%edi_). Don\'t trust the upper half.

`long`:

:   A `long` is an integer number of 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux (but 4
    bytes on 64-bit Windows), from _-9,223,372,036,854,775,808_ to
    _9,223,372,036,854,775,807_ (Rust `i64`; Python `ctypes.c_long`).
    It is the size of a register and of our `.quad` numbers. `long long`
    is also 8 bytes.

`float`:

:   A `float` is a floating-point number of 4 bytes (Rust `f32`;
    Python `ctypes.c_float`). Floating-point numbers will be explained
    in more depth in
    [Floating-point Numbers](10-counting-like-a-computer.qmd#floating-point-numbers).

`double`:

:   A `double` is a floating-point number of 8 bytes, more precise than
    a `float` (Rust `f64`; Python `ctypes.c_double`, or simply a Python
    `float`).

`unsigned`:

:   `unsigned` is a modifier used for any of the above integer types
    which keeps them from being used as signed quantities, for example
    `unsigned long` (Rust `u64`). The difference between signed and
    unsigned numbers will be discussed in
    [Chapter 10. Counting Like a Computer](10-counting-like-a-computer.qmd#chapter-10-counting-like-a-computer).
    `size_t` is an `unsigned long` used for sizes and lengths (Rust
    `usize`).

`*`:

:   An asterisk (`*`) is used to denote that the data isn\'t an actual
    value, but instead is a pointer to a location holding the given
    value. Every pointer is 8 bytes, an address. So, let\'s say in
    memory location `my_location` you have the number 20 stored. If the
    prototype said to pass a `long`, you would load the value with
    `movq my_location(%rip), %rdi`. However, if the prototype said to
    pass a `long *`, you would load the address of the value with
    `leaq my_location(%rip), %rdi`. In addition to indicating the
    address of a single value, pointers can also be used to pass a
    sequence of consecutive locations, starting with the one pointed to
    by the given value. This is called an array. In Rust, a pointer is
    `*const T` or `*mut T`; in Python, `ctypes.POINTER(T)`, or
    `ctypes.c_char_p` for strings.

`struct`:

:   A `struct` is a set of data items that have been put together under
    a name, like the records of Chapter 6. For example you could
    declare:

    ```{.c}
    struct teststruct {
        int a;
        char *b;
    };
    ```

    And any time you ran into `struct teststruct` you would know that it
    is actually an integer and a pointer to a character or group of
    characters. In memory, the integer takes 4 bytes, then come 4
    unused bytes, and then the 8-byte pointer, because each member must
    be at an address that is a multiple of its size. Rust uses the same
    layout when the struct is marked `#[repr(C)]`. Structs are rarely
    passed to functions directly; usually you see pointers to structs
    passed as arguments, because a struct can take up a lot of space.

`typedef`:

:   A `typedef` basically allows you to rename a type. For example, I
    can do `typedef long myowntype;` in a C program, and any time I
    typed `myowntype`, it would be just as if I typed `long` (Rust does
    the same with `type MyOwnType = i64;`). This can get kind of
    annoying, because you have to look up what all of the typedefs and
    structs in a function prototype really mean. However, `typedef`s
    are useful for giving types more meaningful and descriptive names.

> **NOTE.**
>
> **Compatibility:**
> The listed sizes are for 64-bit Linux on x86-64 and most other 64-bit
> Unix systems, where `long` and pointers are 8 bytes. Other systems use
> other sizes (on 64-bit Windows, `long` is 4 bytes). When the size
> matters, libraries use types with the size in the name, such as
> `int64_t` and `uint8_t`, which mean the same everywhere.

That\'s how to read function documentation. Now, let\'s get back to the
question of how to find out about libraries. Most of your system
libraries are in `/usr/lib` or `/lib` and their subdirectories (such as
`/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` on Ubuntu). If you want to just see what
functions and variables they offer, run `objdump -T FILENAME` where
`FILENAME` is the full path to the library. The output of that isn\'t
too helpful, though, for finding an interface that you might need.
Usually, you have to know what library you want at the beginning, and
then just read the documentation. Most libraries have manuals or man
pages for their functions: `man 3 printf` describes `printf` (section 3
of the manual is for library functions, section 2 for system calls).
The web is the best source of documentation for libraries. Most
libraries from the GNU project also have info pages on them, which are
a little more thorough than man pages.

Useful Functions {#useful-functions}
----------------

Several useful functions you will want to be aware of from the C
library include:

-   `size_t strlen(const char *s)`{.c} calculates the size of
    null-terminated strings.

-   `int strcmp(const char *s1, const char *s2)`{.c} compares two
    strings alphabetically.

-   `char *strdup(const char *s)`{.c} takes the pointer to a string,
    and creates a new copy in a new location, and returns the new
    location.

-   `FILE *fopen(const char *filename, const char *opentype)`{.c}
    opens a managed, buffered file (allows easier reading and writing
    than using file descriptors directly).[^8-3] [^8-4]

-   `int fclose(FILE *stream)`{.c} closes a file opened with `fopen`.

-   `char *fgets(char *s, int count, FILE *stream)`{.c} fetches a
    line of characters into string `s`.

-   `int fputs(const char *s, FILE *stream)`{.c} writes a string to
    the given open file.

-   `int fprintf(FILE *stream, const char *template, ...)`{.c} is
    just like `printf`, but it uses an open file rather than defaulting
    to using standard output.

You can find the complete manual on this library by going to
[The GNU C Library manual][8-GNU-Libc].

How a Call Reaches the Library {#how-a-call-reaches-the-library}
------------------------------

Let\'s see now what `@PLT` means. When the linker builds our program, it
doesn\'t know where the C library will be loaded, so it can\'t put the
address of `printf` in our `call`. Instead, it adds two small tables to
the program: the *procedure linkage table* (PLT), with a few
instructions for each library function, and the *global offset table*
(GOT), with an 8-byte slot for the address of each one. Our `call`
jumps to the PLT entry, and the PLT entry jumps to the address that is
in the GOT slot. The dynamic linker only has to fill the GOT; the code
of the program is never changed. `call printf@PLT` asks the assembler
for exactly that: a call to the PLT entry of `printf`.

`objdump -d` shows the result. This is part of its output for
`008-02-printf-example` (with `--no-show-raw-insn`, which hides the
bytes of each instruction):

    0000000000401010 <printf@plt>:
      401010:   jmp    *0x1fea(%rip)        # 403000 <printf@GLIBC_2.2.5>
      401016:   push   $0x0
      40101b:   jmp    401000 <printf@plt-0x10>

    ...

    0000000000401030 <_start>:
      401030:   lea    0x1fd9(%rip),%rdi        # 403010 <first_string>
      ...
      401053:   call   401010 <printf@plt>

The `call` goes to `printf@plt`, and its first instruction jumps to the
address stored at `403000`, the GOT slot of `printf`. Notice that this
`jmp` uses _%rip_-relative addressing too, and that it has a `*`: it
jumps to the address *stored* in that memory, not to the memory itself.
The other two instructions are used the first time: the slot initially
points back to them, and they ask the dynamic linker to find `printf`,
store its address in the slot and jump there. The following calls go
straight to `printf`. This is called *lazy binding*.[^8-5]

`objdump -R` lists the slots that the dynamic linker has to fill, the
*dynamic relocations* of the program:

```{.bash}
objdump -R 008-02-printf-example
```

```
008-02-printf-example:     file format elf64-x86-64

DYNAMIC RELOCATION RECORDS
OFFSET           TYPE              VALUE
0000000000403000 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT  printf@GLIBC_2.2.5
0000000000403008 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT  exit@GLIBC_2.2.5
```

`GLIBC_2.2.5` is the version of each function: the first version of the
GNU C library for x86-64. A library can keep the old version of a
function for old programs while new programs get a new one.

Building a Shared Library {#building-a-shared-library}
-------------------------

Let\'s say that we wanted to take all of our shared code from
[Chapter 6. Reading and Writing Simple Records](06-reading-and-writing-simple-records.qmd#chapter-6-reading-and-writing-simple-records)
and build it into a shared library to use in our programs. The first
thing we would do is assemble them like normal:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 006-01-write-record.o 006-01-write-record.s
as --64 -g -o 006-01-read-record.o 006-01-read-record.s
```

Now, instead of linking them into a program, we want to link them into a
shared library. This changes our linker command to this:

```{.bash}
ld -shared -o librecord.so 006-01-write-record.o 006-01-read-record.o
```

This links both of these files together into a shared library called
`librecord.so`. This file can now be used for multiple
programs. If we need to update the functions contained within it, we can
just update this one file and not have to worry about which programs use
it.

Let\'s look at how we would link against this library. To link the
`006-01-write-records` program of Chapter 6 with it, we would do the
following:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 006-01-write-records.o 006-01-write-records.s
ld -o 008-03-write-records 006-01-write-records.o \
  -L . -l record -dynamic-linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
```

In this command, `-L .` (or `--library-path .`) told the linker to look
for libraries in the current directory (it usually only searches the
system directories, such as `/lib` and `/usr/lib`). As we\'ve seen, the
option `-dynamic-linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2` specified the
dynamic linker. The option `-l record` tells the linker to search for
functions in the file named `librecord.so`. The program doesn\'t need
`-l c`, because it doesn\'t use the C library.

Now the `008-03-write-records` program is built, but it will not run.
If we try it, we will get this error (and the exit status 127):

    ./008-03-write-records: error while loading shared libraries: librecord.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory

This is because, by default, the dynamic linker only searches the
system directories, and whatever directories are listed in
`/etc/ld.so.conf`, for libraries. In order to run the program, you
either need to move the library to one of these directories, or execute
the following command:

```{.bash}
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./008-03-write-records
```

Setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` tells the dynamic linker to add whatever
paths you give it to the library search path for shared libraries.
Written before the command, as above, it only applies to that command.
To set it for the rest of the session (until the terminal is closed),
export it:

```{.bash}
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=.
```

Now, you can run `008-03-write-records` normally by typing
`./008-03-write-records`. It creates the same `test.dat` as
`006-01-write-records`. Let\'s print the shared object dependencies of
`008-03-write-records`:

```{.bash}
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ldd ./008-03-write-records
```

It will report back something like:

    linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007f53f7fcf000)
    librecord.so => ./librecord.so (0x00007f53f7fc4000)

The C library doesn\'t appear: neither the program nor `librecord.so`
use it. And this is the `objdump -R` result:

```{.bash}
objdump -R ./008-03-write-records
```

```
./008-03-write-records:     file format elf64-x86-64

DYNAMIC RELOCATION RECORDS
OFFSET           TYPE              VALUE
0000000000403000 R_X86_64_JUMP_SLOT  write_record
```

Our function is reached through the PLT, just like `printf`. Our
`call write_record` didn\'t say `@PLT`: for a call to a function that
isn\'t in the same file, the assembler creates the same kind of
reference anyway (you can see it with `readelf -r`, as the relocation
type `R_X86_64_PLT32`), and the linker decides whether the call goes to
a PLT entry or directly to the function. Writing `@PLT` simply makes the
intent clear, and the programs of this book write it for every library
function.

Position-Independent Code {#position-independent-code}
-------------------------

A shared library is loaded at a different address in every program, and
in every run. So its code can\'t contain any absolute address: if
`librecord.so` had an instruction like `movq $buffer, %rax` with the
address of its `buffer` written into it, that address would only be
right at one place in memory. Code that works at any address is called
*position-independent code*, or *PIC*, and every shared library has to
be made of it.

This is the reason why this book reaches data relative to _%rip_ since
Chapter 3. The distance from an instruction to the data it uses is
fixed when the library is linked, wherever the library is loaded, so
`leaq buffer(%rip), %rax` gives the right address everywhere. The
program `003-03-maximum-absolute` from the box \"Absolute Addresses and
PIE\" in Chapter 3 uses absolute addresses on purpose; try to put it in
a shared library:

```{.bash}
ld -shared -o absolute.so 003-03-maximum-absolute.o
```

`ld` refuses:

    ld: 003-03-maximum-absolute.o: relocation R_X86_64_32S against `.data' can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC
    ld: failed to set dynamic section sizes: bad value

`-fPIC` is the option that tells a C compiler to generate
position-independent code; in assembly, it is our job.

There is one more detail, and it has to do with data. The following
function, `008-04-call-count.s`, will be part of a library. It counts
how many times it is called, in a variable of its own, `calls`:

```{.gnuassembler .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-04-call-count.s}
```

The variable is reached relative to _%rip_, and it works. But try
adding the line `.globl calls`, which makes the variable visible to
other files, and link the library again:

    ld: global.o: warning: relocation against `calls' in read-only section `.text'
    ld: global.o: relocation R_X86_64_PC32 against symbol `calls' can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC
    ld: final link failed: bad value

The address is still relative to _%rip_, so what is wrong? A global name
in a shared library can be *replaced*: if the program, or a library
loaded before this one, also defines `calls`, the dynamic linker uses
that definition everywhere, including inside our library. The
`LD_PRELOAD` exercise at the end of this chapter uses exactly that to
replace a function of the C library. Then `calls` wouldn\'t be at a
fixed distance from our code, and `ld` won\'t pretend it is. There are
two ways out. If the variable is private to the library, keep it local
(without `.globl`), as `008-04-call-count.s` does. If it must be global,
or if it belongs to another library, read its address from the GOT:

```{.gnuassembler}
    movq  calls@GOTPCREL(%rip), %rax  # %rax = &calls
    incq  (%rax)
```

`calls@GOTPCREL(%rip)` is the GOT slot that holds the address of
`calls`, which the dynamic linker fills; the solution of the exercise
that rewrites `005-01-toupper` with the C library uses it to reach the
C library\'s `stderr`. Functions have the same issue, but `@PLT`
already solves it, since the call goes through the GOT.

Programs can be position-independent too. Such a program is called a
*position-independent executable*, or PIE, and Linux loads it at a
random address, like a library. Compilers produce PIE programs by
default today, and `ld -pie` links ours that way: since all of our
data is reached relative to _%rip_, they work without changes. One
detail: unless you tell it otherwise, `ld -pie` writes into the program
the name of a dynamic linker that Linux distributions don\'t have, and
the program fails with `cannot execute: required file not found`. Name
the real one with `-dynamic-linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, as for
the programs that use the C library, or, for a program that uses no
library at all, add `--no-dynamic-linker` (Chapter 9 does this). Your
first PIE program is in the next section.

Calling Assembly from Rust and Python {#calling-assembly-from-rust-and-python}
-------------------------------------

A shared library doesn\'t care which language its callers are written
in. Let\'s put two assembly functions in a library, `count_chars` from
Chapter 6 (it returns the length of a null-terminated string) and
`call_count` from the previous section:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 006-01-count-chars.o 006-01-count-chars.s
as --64 -g -o 008-04-call-count.o 008-04-call-count.s
ld -shared -o libbook.so 006-01-count-chars.o 008-04-call-count.o
```

`objdump -T` shows the functions that the library offers:

```
libbook.so:     file format elf64-x86-64

DYNAMIC SYMBOL TABLE:
0000000000001000 g    DF .text  0000000000000000 count_chars
0000000000001024 g    DF .text  0000000000000000 call_count
```

Only the global names are there. `calls` is not, so nobody outside the
library can see it or replace it.

This Rust program, `008-05-use-library.rs`, calls both functions:

```{.rust .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-05-use-library.rs}
```

`unsafe extern "C"` declares functions that exist somewhere else and
follow the system calling convention, which Rust calls `"C"`. They are
declared the way a prototype would declare them: `count_chars` receives
a pointer to characters and returns an unsigned 64-bit number, which
Rust expects in _%rax_. Rust can\'t check that the library really has
these functions with these parameters, so each call has to be written
inside an `unsafe` block: the programmer promises that the declaration
is right. The `c"hello world"` literal is a string with a null byte at
the end, exactly what `count_chars` expects. Build it with `rustc`, the
Rust compiler, which also accepts `-L` and `-l`:

```{.bash}
rustc --edition 2024 -L . -l book -o 008-05-use-library \
  008-05-use-library.rs
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./008-05-use-library
```

With Rust 1.100.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 it prints:

    count_chars("hello world") = 11
    call_count() = 1
    call_count() = 2
    call_count() = 3

The value of `calls` stayed in the library between the calls. `ldd`
shows that the Rust program uses our library and the C library, like
almost every Linux program:

    linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007ff3bd0d9000)
    libbook.so => ./libbook.so (0x00007ff3bd077000)
    libgcc_s.so.1 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgcc_s.so.1 (0x00007ff3bd046000)
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007ff3bce00000)
    /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007ff3bd0db000)

`rustc` builds PIE programs, so this is the PIE program we promised.
The `rustc` command uses the system\'s C compiler (`cc`) to link, so it
needs one installed (on Ubuntu, the package `build-essential`).

Python doesn\'t need to be compiled at all. Its `ctypes` module loads a
shared library while the program runs and calls its functions. This is
`008-06-use-library.py`:

```{.python .numberLines include=resource/asm/008-06-use-library.py}
```

```{.bash}
python3 008-06-use-library.py
```

It prints the same four lines (Python 3.12). `ctypes.CDLL` loads the
library; it needs a path with a `/`, here the absolute path, because a
bare name like `libbook.so` is only searched in the standard places,
like with the dynamic linker. Then the program describes each function:
`argtypes` lists the types of the parameters, so that `ctypes` can
convert Python values (here, a `bytes` string becomes the address of
its characters, followed by a null byte), and `restype` is the type of
the result. A shared library doesn\'t record the types of its
functions, so this description is the program\'s job, as it was in
Rust. Without `restype`, `ctypes` assumes that the function returns an
`int`, 4 bytes, and would throw away the upper half of _%rax_.

That is the real use of the calling convention: the same machine code,
in the same library, is called from assembly language, from Rust and
from Python.

More Information about Shared Libraries {#more-information-about-shared-libraries}
---------------------------------------

For further information about dynamic linking, see the following
sources:

-   The man page for `ld.so` contains a lot of information about how the
    Linux dynamic linker works: `man 8 ld.so`.

-   The [System V AMD64 psABI][8-ABI], the document that defines the
    calling convention, also defines the PLT, the GOT and the
    relocation types such as `R_X86_64_PLT32`.

-   Introduction to the ELF Format:
    [The ELF Header][8-Elf-Makan-01],
    [Understanding Program Headers][8-Elf-Makan-02],
    [The Section Headers][8-Elf-Makan-03],
    [Exploring Section Types and Special Sections][8-Elf-Makan-04],
    [Understanding C start up][8-Elf-Makan-05],
    [The Symbol Table and Relocations: Part I][8-Elf-Makan-06-01],
    [The Symbol Table and Relocations: Part II][8-Elf-Makan-06-02],
    [More Relocation tricks: Part III][8-Elf-Makan-06-03]
    and
    [Dynamic Linking / Loading and the .dynamic section][8-Elf-Makan-07]
    provide a good introduction to the ELF file format.

-   Executable and Linkable Format 101:
    [Part 1: Sections and Segments][8-Elf-101-01],
    [Part 2: Symbols][8-Elf-101-02] and
    [Part 3: Relocations][8-Elf-101-03] contains a great
    description of how dynamic linking works with ELF files.
    [Part 4: Dynamic Linking][8-Elf-101-04]
    is a great presentation on dynamic linking in Linux.

-   [Program Library HOWTO Shared Libraries][8-shared-libraries]
    contains a good introduction to shared libraries under Linux.

-   The chapter [FFI][8-Rust-FFI] of *The Rustonomicon* and the
    documentation of [ctypes][8-Python-ctypes] explain how Rust and
    Python call code in other languages.

Review {#review-6}
------

### Know the Concepts {#know-the-concepts-6}

-   What are the advantages and disadvantages of shared libraries?

-   Given a library named \'foo\', what would the library\'s filename
    be?

-   What does the `ldd` command do?

-   Let\'s say we had the files `foo.o` and `bar.o`, and you wanted to
    link them together, and dynamically link them to the library
    \'kramer\'. What would the linking command be to generate the final
    executable?

-   What is *typedef* for?

-   What are *struct*s for?

-   What is the difference between a data element of type *long* and
    *long \**? How would you access them differently in your program?

-   If you had an object file called `foo.o`, what would be the command
    to create a shared library called \'bar\'?

-   What is the purpose of LD_LIBRARY_PATH?

-   What two rules must a program follow before it calls `printf`?

-   What are the PLT and the GOT for?

-   Why must the code of a shared library be position-independent?

### Use the Concepts {#use-the-concepts-6}

-   Rewrite one or more of the programs from the previous chapters to
    print their results to the screen using `printf` rather than
    returning the result as the exit status code. Also, make the exit
    status code be 0.

-   Use the `factorial` function you developed in
    [Recursive Functions](04-all-about-functions.qmd#recursive-functions)
    to make a shared library. Then re-write the main program so that it
    links with the library dynamically.

-   Rewrite the program above so that it also links with the C library.
    Use the C library\'s `printf` function to display the result of the
    `factorial` call.

-   Call the `factorial` function of your library from Python with
    `ctypes`.

-   Rewrite the `005-01-toupper` program so that it uses the C library
    functions for files rather than system calls.

### Going Further {#going-further-6}

-   Make a list of all the environment variables used by the GNU/Linux
    dynamic linker.

-   Research the different types of executable file formats in use today
    and in the history of computing. Tell the strengths and weaknesses
    of each.

-   What kinds of programming are you interested in (graphics,
    databases, science, etc.)? Find a library for working in that area,
    and write a program that makes some basic use of that library.

-   Research the use of `LD_PRELOAD`. What is it used for? Try building
    a shared library that contained the `exit` function, and have it
    write a message to STDERR before exiting. Use `LD_PRELOAD` and run
    various programs with it. What are the results?

[^8-1]: Each of these terms have slightly different meanings, but most
    people use them interchangeably anyway. *DLL* is the name used on
    Windows, and *shared object* (hence `.so`) the name used on Linux.

[^8-2]: The 32-bit convention passed every parameter on the stack, in
    reverse order, so that the format string was always at the top,
    in a known position, whatever the number of parameters. In the
    64-bit convention, the first parameter is always in _%rdi_, which
    solves the same problem.

[^8-3]: `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` (all lower case) can be used in
    these programs to refer to the files of their corresponding file
    descriptors. They are variables of the C library that hold a
    `FILE *`.

[^8-4]: `FILE` is a struct. You don\'t need to know its contents to use
    it. You only have to store the pointer and pass it to the relevant
    other functions.

[^8-5]: Many distributions link their programs with `-z now`, which
    tells the dynamic linker to fill every slot before the program
    starts, and with `-z relro`, which makes the GOT read-only after
    that, so that an attacker who can write to memory can\'t redirect a
    library call. The environment variable `LD_BIND_NOW=1` asks for the
    first part, filling every slot before the program starts, in any
    program.
